summary:
Queensland is a state within Australia and stands under the national framework: the federal Sex Discrimination Act has protected gender identity since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that this protection extends to trans women as women and awarded damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member; Reuters reported the decision on 23 August 2024 as a national precedent on the exclusion of trans women from services under sex-discrimination law. The dispute arose out of organised exclusionary activism.

Federal hate-crime legislation (Act 1 of 2025) passed in February 2025 and took effect immediately, explicitly covering sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment. Vilification coverage at state level remains uneven across Australia: Queensland is one of the jurisdictions whose law covers gender identity, alongside South Australia and Tasmania, while New South Wales, the ACT and Victoria cover only sexual orientation and the Northern Territory and Western Australia cover neither.

Queensland's own discrimination law strengthened on 29 April 2024, when amendments commenced that moved serious vilification out of the Anti-Discrimination Act and into the Criminal Code, raising the maximum penalty from six months to three years' imprisonment. Those amendments explicitly extend protection to non-binary and gender-diverse people and broaden the definition of gender identity, as stated by the Queensland Human Rights Commission. The Commission has separately presented its account of the Anti-Discrimination Bill 2024 rewrite as a modernised gender identity attribute alongside revised vilification provisions.

Queensland was the first Australian state to criminalise conversion practices. The Health Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 passed the Queensland Parliament on 13 August 2020, criminalising electro-shock, drug and hypnotherapy practices aimed at changing a person's sexuality or gender identity, with fines and jail time for practitioners. Survivors told SBS the ban does not reach conversion practices in informal, non-healthcare settings.

Entry, facilities and relationship recognition carry no restriction: no Australian law confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 came into force on 9 December 2017 after a 61.6% Yes result in the national postal survey. Federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto partners since 2009, and overseas same-sex marriages are recognised automatically.

Care access for trans young people is the adverse measure in force for this visit window. In January 2025 Health Minister Tim Nicholls halted puberty blockers and hormone therapy for new public-system patients under 18 with gender dysphoria, formalised by a Queensland Health directive of 28 January 2025 that exempts patients already registered at the Queensland Children's Gender Service. The Queensland Supreme Court ruled the directive unlawful on 27 October 2025; a new ministerial directive reinstated substantially the same restrictions on 28 October 2025 pending reviews, and a legal challenge was filed in December 2025. Equality Australia has called Queensland an outlier state, and families affected by the pause report private treatment costs of hundreds of dollars per injection, approaching $2,000 in one case.

Detention runs on a stated rule with discretion attached. Queensland's inspection standards of August 2023, issued under the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender, but staff retain discretion at admission and transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that identity-based process. The 2009 Corrective Services procedure it replaced was assessed as largely ineffective.
tangentialFactors:
Vilification protection differs sharply between Australian jurisdictions, so conduct treated as an offence in Queensland may not be elsewhere. Victoria's Anti-vilification Act 2025 carries gender identity among its grounds but does not take effect until 30 June 2026, while the New South Wales, ACT and Victorian provisions cover sexual orientation only.

A New South Wales independent review released in September 2024 found puberty blockers safe, effective and reversible while calling for more long-term research, a finding that contrasts with Queensland's restrictions on the same treatments. New South Wales has also passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024, and the broader national direction of travel has been toward protection rather than restriction outside the youth-care measures.

The Tickle v Giggle litigation grew out of organised exclusionary activism targeting a trans woman's membership of a female-only service, indicating that private gatekeeping of women-only spaces remains a live source of dispute even where no statute requires exclusion.

Two sources in the record are not reachable on their live pages: the Queensland Human Rights Commission announcement behind the Anti-Discrimination Bill 2024 account, and the New South Wales Parliament bill document. Both rest on the record held here rather than a page that can currently be loaded.
localsOnly:
Queensland residents gain a higher vilification ceiling from the 29 April 2024 amendments: serious vilification now sits in the Criminal Code at a maximum of three years' imprisonment, against six months previously, and the protection is written to cover non-binary and gender-diverse people expressly.

The conversion-practices ban binds Queensland practitioners in health settings but does not cover informal, non-healthcare settings, according to survivors interviewed by SBS after the Health Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 passed on 13 August 2020. The gap is a matter of scope in the statute, not enforcement.

The puberty-blocker and hormone pause applies to new patients entering the Queensland public system; patients already registered at the Queensland Children's Gender Service were exempted by the 28 January 2025 directive. Families who fall outside that exemption report paying hundreds of dollars per injection privately, with one case near $2,000, and the restrictions remain legally contested through the challenge filed in December 2025.

For prisoners, the August 2023 inspection standards direct placement according to lived or experienced gender but leave admission decisions to staff discretion, and people who have had sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that identity-based assessment. The 2009 Corrective Services procedure these standards replaced was itself assessed as largely ineffective.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the legal challenge filed in December 2025 against Queensland's 28 October 2025 ministerial directive is not sourced here; the record establishes that the challenge was filed and that the directive is in force pending reviews.

Whether the Anti-Discrimination Bill 2024 described by the Queensland Human Rights Commission has been enacted in the form the Commission presents, and the current status of any further rewrite, is unresolved: the Commission's announcement is no longer reachable and the record relies on the account held here.

The New South Wales Parliament bill document supporting the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024 would not load, so that reference rests on the record rather than a live page. Whether the informal, non-healthcare setting gap in Queensland's conversion-practices ban has since been closed by amendment is not sourced.

Access to gender-affirming care in Queensland's private system, as distinct from the public directives, is not covered by the sources held here.
